merger_description:
Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited (**Sun Pharma**), through a wholly owned subsidiary Sun Pharma America, Inc., proposes to acquire 100% of the shares of Organon & Co. (**Organon**) (**Acquisition**).

Sun Pharma is a global specialty generics pharmaceutical company present in over 100 countries. Sun Pharma's portfolio includes cardiology, psychiatry, neurology, gastroenterology and dermatology. In Australia, Sun Pharma is involved in the supply and distribution of drugs across (i) patented medicines, (ii) retail/hospital Sun Pharma branded generics, and (iii) white label generics.

Organon is a global healthcare company present in 140 countries and territories. Its portfolio is focused on women's health, biosimilars, and general medicines.

In Australia, the parties overlap in the supply of statins, selective serotonin agonists for migraine treatment, atypical antipsychotics, antidepressants and mood stabilisers.

The parties also overlap in the supply of antigonadotropin-releasing hormones, specifically in the supply of ganirelix acetate (**ganirelix**), a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (**GnRH**) antagonist used in in vitro fertilisation (**IVF**) protocols to prevent premature ovulation.

* Organon supplies Orgalutran, the originator ganirelix product, which went off patent in Australia in 2018. Orgalutran is manufactured by a third party and distributed in Australia by Alphapharm Pty Ltd.
* Sun Pharma was the first to enter the generic ganirelix market in Australia in 2021 with Ganirelix SUN.

With respect to the supply of ganirelix, Sun Pharma has expanded its existing global ganirelix outlicencing arrangement with Ferring Pharmaceuticals B.V. (**Ferring**) to Australia (the **Ferring Agreement**). Under this arrangement, Sun Pharma has agreed to grant exclusive commercialisation, distribution, marketing and sales rights for Ganirelix SUN in Australia to Ferring. Ferring will take over the commercialisation activities of Ganirelix SUN from 1 December 2026 after the transfer is completed. Sun Pharma will continue to manufacture Ganirelix SUN to supply to Ferring. Sun Pharma has provided a summary document of the Ferring Agreement which is attached below.

Sun Pharma also has a pipeline cetrorelix acetate product, which has applied for PBS listing and is a GnRH antagonist.

determination_table_content.details: The reasons for the ACCC’s determination are set out in section 2.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines and interim merger process guidelines.

In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered the information and documents that were submitted with the notification form, additional information provided by the parties to the Acquisition (the Parties), market feedback and publicly available information.
For the reasons given below, the ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into effect.
Industry background
Pharmaceutical supply chain
Based on information currently before it, the ACCC understands that the supply of pharmaceutical products in Australia generally involves:

items: Manufacturers: Pharmaceutical products can be manufactured in-house or through third party contract manufacturing organisations, or a combination of both. Manufacturers can supply products to distributors and wholesalers, and can also contract directly with pharmacies and hospitals.

Distributors: Manufacturers may enter into third-party distribution arrangements under which distributors price, market, distribute and/or sell pharmaceutical products to wholesalers, pharmacies and hospitals.
Wholesalers: Wholesalers stock and distribute pharmaceutical products from manufacturers or distributors to pharmacies and hospitals.

Prescribers (primarily doctors): Prescribers determine the most clinically appropriate pharmaceutical product for each patient and write prescriptions by reference to the molecule name or active pharmaceutical ingredient (but can also specify the brand to be dispensed and, if so, can indicate whether generic substitution is not permitted by ticking the relevant box on the prescription).1

Pharmacies and hospitals (dispensers): Pharmaceutical products are typically dispensed to patients through pharmacies, which may enter supply agreements across a portfolio of products or procure products on a line-by-line basis, or hospitals, which typically procure products through competitive tender processes conducted on an active ingredient basis.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: Classification of pharmaceutical products

Pharmaceutical products can be classified by reference to the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system, a hierarchical and coded 4 level drug classification system developed and maintained by the European Pharmaceutical Market Research Association.2

The broadest level, ATC 1, divides pharmaceutical products into 16 anatomical main groups. The second level, ATC 2, is either a pharmacological or therapeutic group. The third level, ATC 3, further groups pharmaceutical products by their specific therapeutic indications (i.e., intended use or treatment indication). The ATC 4 level is the chemical, pharmacological or therapeutic subgroup. The World Health Organisation’s adjusted ATC system has adopted a fifth level, ATC 5, which is the molecule level.3 1 See https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/active-ingredient-prescribing. 2 See https://www.ephmra.org/anatomical-classification and EphMRA’s Anatomical Classification Guidelines at https://www.ephmra.org/sites/default/files/2026-01/2026%20ATC%20Guidlines%20Final.pdf. 3 See: https://www.who.int/tools/atc-ddd-toolkit/atc-classification.
Regulatory landscape and pharmaceutical pricing

Unless exempt, therapeutic goods cannot be supplied in Australia unless they are included on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG). Once a medicine is listed on the ARTG, manufacturers and/or suppliers can apply for Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) listing.

The PBS is an Australian government program that subsidises the cost of certain medicines. Under the PBS, a listed medicine cannot be priced above its regulated Approved Ex-Manufacturer Price (AEMP) for a PBS-subsidised supply. Generic and originator brands face the same AEMP, unless the originator has applied for a brand premium. When an originator product is first listed on the PBS, the AEMP is negotiated and set with the Department of Health. When the first generic version of a product is listed, this triggers a statutory 25% price reduction to the AEMP.

Further price reductions then occur through an ongoing price disclosure regime. Under this regime, brand pricing and volume data (including the value of discounts and rebates offered to pharmacies) is used to calculate the weighted average disclosed price (WADP) of a medicine. Where the current price of a medicine exceeds the WADP by a prescribed threshold, this triggers a price reduction.4
Relevant areas of competition
Overlap in the supply of ganirelix in Australia
The Parties overlap in the supply of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists, specifically ganirelix acetate (ganirelix), for use in in vitro fertilisation (IVF) protocols in Australia.

GnRH antagonists are used in IVF protocols to prevent premature ovulation and allow clinicians to control the timing of egg collection. There are two GnRH antagonists approved for use in IVF protocols in Australia: ganirelix and cetrorelix. Ganirelix and cetrorelix share the same chemical sub-group (i.e. they overlap at the ATC 4 level) but differ at the molecular (ATC 5) level. This means that prescribers can prescribe ganirelix or cetrorelix for the same indication, however dispensers cannot substitute them and must dispense the molecule prescribed. Ganirelix and cetrorelix are typically prescribed in Australia at IVF clinics.

Organon supplies the originator ganirelix product, Orgalutran, which was registered on the ARTG on 19 March 2001. The patent for Orgalutran expired in Australia in 2018. The Orgalutran active pharmaceutical ingredient is manufactured by a third party, with Organon subsequently packaging the finished dosage form (i.e. preparing it into a final form ready for administration). Organon supplies Orgalutran to Alphapharm Pty Ltd trading as Viatris (Alphapharm), which acts as Organon’s exclusive distributor of Orgalutran in Australia. However, Organon continues to market Orgalutran directly to IVF clinics.

Sun Pharma supplies Ganirelix SUN, which was the first generic ganirelix product made available in Australia following the expiry of the Orgalutran patent. Ganirelix SUN was registered on the ARTG on 2 November 2020 and PBS listing on 1 April 4 See: https://www.pbs.gov.au/industry/pricing/price-disclosure-spd 2021. Sun Pharma manufactures, packages the finished dosage form and distributes Ganirelix SUN.

On 16 July 2026, Sun Pharma amended an existing global Supply and Distribution Agreement with Ferring Pharmaceutical B.V. (Ferring)5 to grant Ferring the exclusive commercialisation, distribution, marketing and sales rights for Ganirelix SUN in Australia (as well as other jurisdictions globally) (the Ferring Agreement). Sun Pharma is transitioning the supply of Ganirelix SUN to Ferring and will continue to manufacture the product for Ferring in the future, though Ferring can request a non- exclusive licence enabling Ferring to seek contract manufacturing from a third party. It is anticipated that Ferring will commence commercialisation activities for Ganirelix SUN by 1 December 2026.6

Sun Pharma has a pipeline generic cetrorelix product, which was listed on the ARTG on 5 March 2025 but is not currently listed on the PBS. There is only one other cetrorelix product available in Australia which is the originator cetrorelix product manufactured and distributed by Merck.

With respect to the broader market for the supply of GnRH antagonists for IVF protocols (i.e. at the ATC 4 level), the ACCC does not consider the Acquisition is likely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition as:

items: Competition between ganirelix and cetrorelix occurs at the prescriber level as they contain different active ingredients and cannot be substituted at the dispensing stage.
Cetrorelix is not commonly prescribed in Australia. Even if Sun Pharma were to enter and capture all cetrorelix sales in Australia, the increment from this would be low.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: As such, the ACCC has focused its competition assessment on the supply of ganirelix in Australia.
Other overlaps

The Parties also overlap in the supply of some statins, selective serotonin agonists for migraine treatment, atypical antipsychotics, antidepressants and mood stabilisers at the ATC 3 and ATC 4 levels (i.e. the products have different active ingredients but may be used to treat similar indications).

The ACCC does not consider the Acquisition is likely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the supply of these products. The increment resulting from the Acquisition would be low for each relevant overlap, and the merged entity would continue to face competition from alternative suppliers of these products. As such, the ACCC has not considered these areas of overlap further in this determination. 5 Ferring is a global pharmaceutical company focusing on reproductive medicine. Ferring has an established presence in the Australian pharmaceutical sector and the Australian IVF segment, with a portfolio of 16 products across reproductive medicine and women’s health, which is distributes nationwide. 6 See Sun Pharma’s submission regarding the Ferring Agreement, 22 October 2026, on the Acquisitions Register.
Competition assessment

The ACCC has considered the effects of the Acquisition by comparing the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition proceeds against the continuation of the current state of competition (being the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition does not proceed).

The ACCC considers that the Acquisition would be unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in relation to the supply of ganirelix in Australia. While the Acquisition would increase the level of concentration, the merged entity would face competition from remaining competitors, including Ferring.
On the evidence before it, the ACCC makes the following findings:

items: Post-Acquisition, the merged entity would have a combined share in the supply of ganirelix in Australia in the range of 80 to 90%.

There may be an enduring market share for the originator product, Orgalutran, with or without the Acquisition, given patient and prescriber preferences for the originator product in IVF protocols. Those preferences may change over time as generic alternatives become better known.
The merged entity would face competition from alternative generic ganirelix suppliers in the future.
Sun Pharma’s ganirelix product would continue to be supplied in Australia, with Ferring acting as an independent competitor to the merged entity in the supply of ganirelix in Australia.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: The basis for these findings is set out in detail below.
Post-Acquisition concentration is high

The Acquisition would combine the 2 largest suppliers of ganirelix in Australia and the merged entity would hold a significant combined market share in the supply of ganirelix post-Acquisition. The combined post-Acquisition share is in the range of 80- 90%.

However, that post-Acquisition share should be considered in the context of Organon’s existing high share, which is in the range of 55-70%. Orgalutran’s share, as the originator product, has been slow to erode since the entry of generic ganirelix alternatives in Australia.

Market feedback indicated that there is some prescriber and patient behaviour that is contributing to a ‘stickiness’ around the use of Orgalutran in IVF protocols, but that this may change over time as prescribers and patients become more comfortable with generic ganirelix alternatives.

Given this ‘stickiness’, the ACCC considers that Orgalutran would likely have an enduring share, with or without the Acquisition. However, as market feedback indicates, this is likely to reduce over time as generic alternatives gain greater acceptance. For that reason, the ACCC has proceeded to consider the competition the merged entity would likely face from suppliers of generic alternatives post- Acquisition.
Effectiveness of remaining competitors
The ACCC considers that the merged entity would face competition from alternative generic suppliers post-Acquisition.
Notably, there is a high degree of substitutability between Orgalutran, Ganirelix SUN and other alternative generic ganirelix products from Arrotex (DBG Health) and Lupin for the following reasons.

items: The products contain the same active ingredient and have demonstrated bioequivalence and comparable quality.7
The products can be legally substituted by pharmacists (unless the prescribing doctor specifically indicates that generic substitution is not permitted on the script).8
The products are subject to the same PBS price (the regulated AEMP),9 with patients paying the same price for each of the products.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: Furthermore, the ACCC understands that suppliers of generic ganirelix products compete to have their generic brand stocked in pharmacies by providing discounts and rebates on their products.10

Competition between generic brands also influences future PBS pricing of ganirelix, as discounts and rebates offered by generic suppliers can reduce the calculated WADP for ganirelix. The level of competition between suppliers of generic ganirelix products consequently affects the level of future price reductions for ganirelix under the PBS.

On the information currently before it, including information obtained from market feedback, the ACCC considers that the merged entity would face a meaningful degree of competition from other generic ganirelix suppliers post-Acquisition, both in terms of competition to supply pharmacies as well as providing some level of competition in respect of PBS pricing. As discussed further below, the ACCC also notes the continuing presence of Sun Pharma’s ganirelix product through Ferring.

For completeness, the ACCC notes that market feedback indicated that the supply of ganirelix in Australia represents a relatively small, low value market, as the application of ganirelix is limited to reproductive treatments and as such, further new entry may be limited. The ACCC has not considered this further in this determination given its conclusion that the merged entity would continue to face competition from existing suppliers. 7 To obtain regulatory approval, suppliers of generic ganirelix products must demonstrate bioequivalence and comparable pharmaceutical quality to Orgalutran. This assessment is conducted by the Therapeutic Goods Administration: Generic prescription medicines: Fact sheet | Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) 8 Ganirelix is 'A-flagged' under the PBS. A pharmaceutical product is ‘A-flagged’ where the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee considers generic versions and the originator to be bioequivalent, such that they can be substituted at the pharmacy level, with the patient’s consent, without returning to the prescriber. 9 Orgalutran has the option to apply for a brand price premium. This higher price would be paid by the patient, not the government. Orgalutran currently does not have a brand price premium applied to it. 10 Information from the Parties and market feedback suggested that pharmacies are the major dispensers of ganirelix, with lower volumes dispensed by hospitals.
The competitive impact of the Ferring agreement

The ACCC has also considered the likely impact of the Ferring Agreement on the supply of ganirelix in Australia.11 Sun Pharma submits that the Ferring Agreement “eliminates the overlap [between the Parties] in ganirelix by establishing Ferring as the exclusive, independent marketer of the ganirelix product manufactured by Sun Pharma in Australia.” 12

Market feedback indicated that Ferring is an established supplier of women’s health products (including IVF treatments) and has existing relationships with IVF clinics. Some market participants expressed the view that the Ferring Agreement will support competition in the supply of ganirelix, whereas others raised concerns that Sun Pharma could degrade the terms of its supply to Ferring or otherwise use the arrangement to its own advantage.

The ACCC considers Ferring is an established pharmaceutical supplier in Australia with an established presence in the IVF sector, and notes that Ferring has successfully commercialised ganirelix manufactured by Sun Pharma in several European countries since 2016.

Having regard to market feedback as well as the terms of the Ferring Agreement, the ACCC considers that Sun Pharma’s ganirelix product would continue to be supplied in Australia with Ferring acting as an independent competitor to the merged entity in the supply of ganirelix in Australia.
